extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of philosophy; readers interested in pragmatism and metaphysics
extracted.subtask_description: Use the pragmatic method to judge metaphysical and abstract concepts by the practical differences they make, especially their consequences for future experience; apply this analysis to problems like God vs. matter, design, free-will, and the one-and-many.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic criterion of meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory or abstract concept is meaningful only insofar as it has alternative practical consequences—i.e., it makes a difference to future experience, however delicate or remote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a metaphysical debate yields no definite future consequences, it is idle and philosophically empty; positivists and scientists rightly ignore such disputes. The 'wise man' should turn his back on theories from which no practical outcomes can be discerned. Pragmatism requires showing alternative practical outcomes to vindicate theoretical discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prospective (future-consequences) test for metaphysical hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge metaphysical hypotheses by the outlooks, hopes, and practical behaviors they prescribe or predict about an unfinished world (i.e., by what they 'promise' about the future).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: materialism and theism may be indistinguishable retrospectively but lead to very different practical expectations about the future (materialism predicts cosmic dissolution and final wreck; theism guarantees an eternal moral order and sustained hope). Thus we should prefer hypotheses that yield a better 'promise' of future outcomes if those consequences matter to us.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional equivalence test (doctrinal substitution only if futures match)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that two terms/concepts (e.g., 'matter' and 'God') are equivalent must be tested by whether they functionally predict the same future tendencies (e.g., permanent moral order, endless melioration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely showing that current past results could be produced by either hypothesis does not suffice; what matters is whether each hypothesis promises similar long-term success or perfection. Mr. Spencer's attempt to re-name God as an unknowable power is pragmatically adequate only if that power promises the same future outcomes a theistic God would.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic interpretation of religious/abstract terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms such as God, Design, Free-will, Spirit, or the Absolute derive their pragmatic meaning from the 'promise' or psychological/evaluative effects they secure (e.g., consolation, confidence, moral holidays), not from abstract definitions alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These terms, when concretely believed, give a 'holiday' or tonic power to life (justify trustful, joyous moments) even before scientific particulars are known. Their precise content must then be worked out by empirical study (we study God by studying Creation), but their immediate pragmatic benefit is the primary meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification requirement for 'design' arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract word 'design' is inert; to be informative one must ask 'what sort of design?' and examine particulars of nature and history to infer the character and purposes of any designer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any actual realized state can be read as 'designed' once its means are shown to fit its result; therefore the bare claim of design explains nothing. To make the design-argument substantive, study the ensemble of particulars (e.g., biological fit, historical sequences like Mont-Pelee) to learn whether the pattern indicates benevolent, diabolical, or other intentions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic account of free-will as novelty and meliorism
rubrics_metrics.description: Free-will should be evaluated by whether it secures genuine novelties in the world — the possibility of improvement (meliorism) — rather than by metaphysical claims about imputability or an enigmatic added faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The moral and social functions of praise and punishment do not depend on metaphysical free-will; instinct and utility suffice for social regulation. The pragmatic value of free-will is that it sustains hope for change and improvement; taken abstractly in a world already perfect, 'freedom' would be meaningless or perverse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total-reflection method for relating abstractions to experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat abstract ideas as elements that interact with the world at its boundary: they are not self-sustaining realities but redirect and re-energize experience when concretely applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the water/air metaphor: abstract ideas (air) are irrespirable alone but, when they touch sensible facts (water), they produce powerful reflections and practical effects. Thus the method is to plunge concepts into the river of experience and observe what changes they effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophic priority of totality (unity + variety)
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy's aim is totality: both the reduction of particulars to system (unity) and acquaintance with the diversity of facts (variety) are indispensable; evaluation must balance systematization and attention to particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstract monism alone (worship of 'one') is inadequate if it suppresses curiosity about particulars. A healthy philosophic approach preserves interest in both the world's unity and its manifold details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational criteria for 'oneness' (modes of practical unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: To make 'the world is one' concrete, examine the different kinds of unity that could matter practically: (a) unity as a single subject of discourse (semantic unity); (b) continuity (space/time) permitting passage across parts; (c) lines of influence (physical, causal, social) that connect elements; (d) superposed systems/networks (acquaintance, postal, commercial) that unify parts locally or globally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each mode of unity has different practical consequences (e.g., continuity grounds motor life; lines of influence allow message propagation; systems create overlapping 'little worlds'). Semantic unity alone has little practical import. Assessments of monism vs pluralism should specify which mode(s) of unity are at stake and what practical effects follow.
